summaries.example: Two students are working on a class garden. Each can help water it or keep playing. Helping takes time, but both students enjoy the healthy garden. If one helps while the other does not, the non-helper gets the benefit without the work. Each student may be tempted not to help, even though both would be happier if they helped together.
summaries.summary: The prisoner’s dilemma is a puzzle about two people who must choose without making a binding agreement. Each person has two choices: cooperate or defect. In the simplest version, defecting is the safer choice for each individual. If the other person cooperates, defecting brings an even better personal result. If the other person defects, defecting is still better than cooperating. Yet when both defect, both do worse than they would have if both had cooperated. This creates a conflict between what seems best for each person separately and what would be best for them together. The same pattern can describe more than a crime story. People may face it when sharing work, protecting a common resource, voting, or paying for something everyone uses. Repeated play changes the situation. A person can remember earlier choices, reward cooperation, or respond to defection. Strategies such as copying a partner’s last move can sometimes support cooperation, although their success depends on the rules, mistakes, and other strategies in the game. The entry also discusses larger groups, optional participation, trust, evolution, social networks, and different ideas about rational choice. These cases show that small changes in information, timing, or rewards can change what happens.
key_ideas: In the basic dilemma, each person may do better by defecting, whatever the other person does.
When both people defect, they can each receive less than they would have received by cooperating.
The dilemma compares individual self-interest with the well-being of a group.
Playing the game repeatedly can make cooperation easier because people can reward helpful actions or respond to harmful ones.
Similar problems can occur in groups, elections, shared resources, and public goods.
There is no single best strategy for every version of the game.
summaries.why_it_matters: The prisoner’s dilemma helps us understand why people who want similar good things may still fail to work together. It can help explain problems involving shared chores, clean air, public safety, voting, and other shared benefits. It also reminds us that cooperation may need trust, communication, repeated interactions, or well-designed rules. The puzzle does not prove that people are selfish or that cooperation is impossible. Instead, it gives us a clear way to ask what conditions make cooperation more likely.

important_terms.definition: A situation where each person has a reason to choose an action that leaves everyone worse off than cooperation would have.
Working together toward a shared goal.
Choosing not to help with the shared goal, often to protect one’s own advantage.
An action that is better for a player no matter what the other player chooses.
A result where neither player can do better by changing alone.

questions_to_think_about: Why might someone choose not to help even when helping together would benefit everyone?
What could make people trust one another?
Would you act differently if you expected to meet the same person many times?
Can rules or fair consequences help a group cooperate?

summaries.example: Suppose two competing firms choose whether to keep prices high or cut prices. If both keep prices high, both earn good profits. If one cuts prices while the other keeps prices high, the price-cutter attracts more customers. If both cut prices, both earn less. Cutting prices is individually attractive in either case, but mutual price-cutting is worse for both than mutual restraint. The example is only a model: its conclusions depend on the payoffs and on whether the firms interact once or repeatedly.
summaries.summary: The prisoner’s dilemma (PD) is a family of strategic situations in which individually rational choices can produce an outcome that all players prefer less than a cooperative alternative. In the standard symmetric two-by-two version, each player chooses cooperate or defect. The payoffs satisfy the ordering temptation > reward > punishment > sucker. Consequently, defection strictly dominates cooperation: regardless of the other player’s action, a player receives a higher payoff by defecting. Mutual defection is therefore the unique strict Nash equilibrium, even though mutual cooperation gives both players more. The entry emphasizes that this formal structure should not be identified too quickly with one moral story. Defection may represent confession, selfishness, refusal to contribute, or a choice not to make a mutually beneficial exchange. The same distinction appears in larger games involving public goods, voting, volunteering, and common resources, though these games may be only PD-like rather than exact PDs. The analysis also distinguishes ordinal from cardinal payoffs and pure from impure dilemmas: with cardinal payoffs and independent randomization, some mixed strategies can sometimes improve on universal cooperation. Timing matters. In an asynchronous game, a later player may condition their action on an earlier action, yet backward reasoning can still produce a poor outcome. In a finite iterated PD, backward induction yields continual defection when rationality and the exact endpoint are common knowledge. Infinite and indefinitely repeated games are different because there is no known final round; a sufficiently valuable future can make reciprocal cooperation an equilibrium. key_ideas: In the standard symmetric two-action PD, defection strictly dominates cooperation, while mutual cooperation is preferred by both to mutual defection.
The mutual-defection outcome is the unique strict Nash equilibrium in the basic game, but equilibrium need not always identify the outcome that is best for everyone.
The dilemma can represent selfish conduct versus altruism, but it can also model mutually beneficial exchange and social cooperation; the labels depend on the payoffs.
Public-goods problems, voting, volunteer shortages, and common-resource problems resemble the PD without always having exactly the same structure.
With a known finite number of rounds, backward induction supports defection in every round under strong rationality and common-knowledge assumptions.
With indefinite or infinite repetition, the absence of a final round can support cooperative equilibria, though outcomes depend on the shadow of the future and the strategies available.
summaries.why_it_matters: The PD matters because it offers a precise model of social dilemmas: situations in which people share an interest in a good outcome but each has an incentive to shift costs onto others. It connects ethics, economics, political theory, decision theory, biology, and computer science. It also shows why there is no universal solution. Cooperation may be supported by repeated encounters, credible responses, communication, partner choice, spatial or social clustering, institutions, or evolutionary dynamics. important_terms.definition: A two-player, two-action game in which each player’s individually dominant action leads to an outcome both players prefer less than mutual cooperation.
An action that gives a player a better outcome than another action in every possible case.
A strategy profile in which no player can improve their payoff by changing strategy alone.
A choice that is at least as good in every case and better in at least one case.
A payoff ranking that tells us which outcomes are preferred but not the size of the differences between them.
A payoff that represents the amount or expected value gained, allowing comparisons of how much better outcomes are.
A repeated game whose continuation is uncertain, often represented by a probability of another round or by discounting future payoffs.
Reasoning backward from the final possible move to earlier moves in a finite game.

questions_to_think_about: Does a Nash equilibrium always deserve to be called the rational solution? Why might equilibrium and mutual benefit come apart?
How do repeated interaction and uncertainty about the final round change the argument for defection?
Is a voting problem really a prisoner’s dilemma if a pivotal vote can make cooperation worthwhile?
Should a strategy be judged by its performance against every opponent or by its performance in a particular population?
How might errors, communication, or the ability to opt out affect cooperation?

summaries.example: Imagine four students planning a group presentation. Each student can do their part or hope that others will do the work. If everyone contributes, the presentation is strong. A student who skips their part may still receive the group grade if others finish it. But if everyone skips, the presentation is poor and everyone receives a worse result. Each student has a reason to free-ride, even though the group would benefit if everyone contributed.
summaries.summary: The prisoner’s dilemma is a philosophical and mathematical model of cooperation. Two or more players choose actions, and the result depends on everyone’s choices. In the familiar two-person version, each player can cooperate or defect. Defection is individually attractive: if the other player cooperates, defection gains the temptation payoff; if the other defects, defection avoids the especially poor sucker payoff. Yet both players receive the punishment payoff when both defect, and each would prefer the reward payoff produced by mutual cooperation. Thus individual rationality can lead to a result that is worse for everyone than coordinated action. The entry examines several interpretations. The game can represent selfish behavior and socially desirable altruism, but it can also describe mutually beneficial exchanges, such as two people trading items they value differently. Larger versions resemble public-goods dilemmas, free-riding, some voting situations, and tragedies involving common resources. These examples do not all share precisely the same formal structure, so their differences matter. The analysis also asks whether equilibrium is always the right solution concept. In a one-shot game, mutual defection is often the only equilibrium. In repeated games, players can use conditional strategies: cooperation can reward cooperation, while defection can trigger a response. In a fixed finite number of rounds, however, backward induction predicts defection throughout if everyone knows the endpoint and everyone’s rationality is common knowledge. Games with an indefinite or unknown continuation differ because future interaction has value. key_ideas: The basic dilemma is a conflict between personal incentives and a result that would benefit everyone.
Mutual defection can be an equilibrium even when both players prefer mutual cooperation.
Not every cooperation problem is exactly a PD; voting, public goods, and shared resources may have similar but different payoff patterns.
Repeated interaction allows rewards, punishments, reputation, and conditional strategies, but cooperation is not guaranteed.
In a finite repeated game, knowing the final round can encourage backward reasoning toward defection.
Uncertainty, mistakes, communication, partner choice, and social networks can alter the strategic situation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The prisoner’s dilemma matters because it explains why agreement about a goal may not be enough to produce cooperation. Group projects, shared resources, public services, voting, and environmental protection can all involve costs that individuals would rather avoid while still receiving the benefits. The model helps us ask what changes the incentives: repeated relationships, reliable information, communication, fair rules, the ability to choose partners, or consequences for exploitation. It also encourages caution. A model can illuminate a situation without proving that people are selfish, that cooperation is always moral, or that one strategy is always best.

important_terms.definition: A strategic situation in which each player’s individually attractive choice leads to a result that all players prefer less than mutual cooperation.
Choosing to help achieve a shared outcome, even when helping has a personal cost.
Choosing the individually safer or more advantageous action instead of helping with the shared outcome.
A strategy that is better than another strategy regardless of what the other player does.
An outcome where no player can improve by changing their choice alone.
A benefit available to everyone, including people who did not help produce it.
A person who receives a shared benefit while avoiding a fair share of its cost.
A game played more than once, so earlier choices can influence later choices.

questions_to_think_about: Is it fair for someone to benefit from a group project without contributing?
Why might a person cooperate when cooperation is not their dominant strategy?
Does meeting someone again give you a good reason to trust them?
When should a voting or environmental problem be called a prisoner’s dilemma, and when is that label too simple?
Can a rule be rational even if following it sometimes gives a person less than taking advantage?
